html:
The Tibetan calendar counts years in cycles of sixty, called rabjung, and the first cycle began in 1027. The date is tied to the arrival in Tibet of the Kalachakra Tantra, the "Wheel of Time" teaching, which brought Indian astronomy and a system of reckoning time.

Each year of the cycle pairs one of twelve animals with one of five elements, wood, fire, earth, iron and water, and each element takes a male and a female year. So 1027 was a fire female rabbit year. The twelve animals and the sixty year count are shared with the Chinese calendar, so the system blends Indian and Chinese ways. Months follow the moon, with an extra month added every two or three years to keep step with the sun, and the New Year, Losar, falls in February or March.

Counting by rabjung lets Tibetan histories date events exactly; the seventeenth cycle began in 1987. The main form of the calendar, the Phugpa system, took shape in the 1400s, and astrologers still issue it each year, including in exile in India. It arrived in the same years as Atisha's mission, during the second spread of Buddhism in Tibet.
